Let’s dive into Chapter 2: The Power of Questions—Moving from Advice to Curiosity. Here’s something you might find surprising—at the heart of the coaching habit is a pretty simple, but powerful, idea. Asking the right questions is often way more valuable than just handing out quick answers. Now, if you’re someone who loves to help, it’s easy to want to jump in and offer advice as soon as a problem pops up. It feels helpful, maybe even efficient. But here’s the catch—it can actually limit real learning, and sometimes, it even makes people rely on you a little too much. Think about what happens when, instead of giving advice, you ask a good question. You invite reflection. You give people a chance to really think for themselves, look at things from new angles, and maybe even come up with solutions that fit them perfectly. It’s not about holding back support. It’s about helping others grow their own problem-solving muscles. Imagine this— there’s a team leader, and a colleague comes by, stressed about hitting a project deadline. The leader’s first instinct? Probably to offer up a quick fix or even jump in and take over. But what if, instead, the leader simply asks, “What’s the real challenge here for you?” Suddenly, the conversation goes deeper. It’s not just about the deadline anymore—it’s about what’s really going on beneath the surface. That question opens the door to honest reflection and self-discovery. Building the habit of asking questions starts with one thing: curiosity. And curiosity means being willing to explore, to really listen, and to hold back on those ready-made solutions. It’s about giving others the space to share and to figure things out for themselves. To make this easy, there’s actually a set of seven essential questions that form the backbone of great coaching. They’re simple, easy to remember, and work in all sorts of situations. These questions help leaders stay curious, keep conversations on track, and avoid slipping into advice mode. Let me walk you through them:
The Kickstart Question: This one opens things up and sets a positive tone. The AWE Question: It’s all about encouraging deeper thought and reflection. The Focus Question: This helps you zero in on what’s really going on. The Foundation Question: It clarifies what the other person actually wants. The Lazy Question: Great for making sure you’re not taking on work you don’t need to. The Strategic Question: Guides the talk toward action and next steps. The Learning Question: This one helps everyone grow and learn from the experience. Each question has its own purpose, shaping the conversation so it’s supportive, but also empowering. The real art lies in knowing when to use them, and in building the habit of listening more than speaking. Of course, building this habit isn’t always easy. It takes self-awareness, a bit of patience, and sometimes, letting go of that urge to be the expert. But the payoff? It’s huge. Teams get stronger, people feel more engaged, and you start to create a culture where learning never really stops. When leaders lean into the power of questions, everything changes. Teams become more resourceful, more confident, and way more capable. Problems get solved in creative ways, and folks feel genuinely valued and understood. So, here’s the key takeaway: The coaching habit isn’t just a toolkit—it’s a whole new way of being that can truly transform the way you lead and connect with others.
